n-m-h1-ineq-03.title: ‘If a<b, then 1/a > 1/b’ — e always true? Make counterexamples

n-m-h1-ineq-03.material: Mina talk, ‘If a<b, then 1/a > 1/b. If 2<5, then 1/2 > 1/5, and if 3<7, then 1/3 > 1/7. I check some examples, and all correct.’ (a and b na nonzero numbers.)

n-m-h1-comb-05.title: Wetin we need know to decide how many ways balls fit go into boxes?

n-m-h1-comb-05.material: Mina ask, "How many ways to put 3 balls into 2 boxes?" Her friends give different answers because the problem miss some details.

n-m-h1-comb-05.s.s2.r.d: That na count when balls are distinct. Balls for this problem all be the same.
n-m-h1-comb-05.s.s2.explain: Split into cases where box 1 get 0, 1, 2, or 3 balls; rest go box 2, so 4 ways. For example, 0 in box 1 means 3 in box 2, and 3 in box 1 means 0 in box 2; different results.
n-m-h1-comb-05.s.s3.prompt: If the 3 balls get different colors and be distinct (boxes still distinct and empty boxes allowed), how many ways? Explain how this relate to the earlier 4 ways too.

n-m-h1-comb-06.title: Explain to my younger brother how to arrange letters in BANANA
n-m-h1-comb-06.topic: Permutations: explain why we divide when identical items dey
n-m-h1-comb-06.goal: Understand why formula for permutations with identical items divide, then rewrite formula-only solution in words a middle-school brother fit understand.
n-m-h1-comb-06.material: Hyunsu solve "number of ways to arrange the 6 letters of BANANA in a row" like this: 6! ÷ (3!×2!) = 720 ÷ 12 = 60 ways. His younger brother, a second-year middle-school student, say, "I no understand why divide, or why na 3! and 2!." (BANANA get 1 B, 3 A, and 2 N.)
n-m-h1-comb-06.thinking.0: Read what each part of the expression count
n-m-h1-comb-06.thinking.1: Rewrite solution for the person wey go read am
n-m-h1-comb-06.thinking.2: Use the same method for other letters
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s1.hint.0: Think how many ways to arrange letters if numbers make dem distinct, like A₁A₂A₃.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s1.hint.1: Use numbered letters to make some arrangements wey look same as BANANA.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s1.o.a: Number of arrangements after treating the identical letters among the 6 letters as removed
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s1.r.a: 6! no include any step for removing identical letters. 6! count by treating all six as different.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s1.o.b: Number of arrangements counted by treating the 3 A and 2 N letters as distinct
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s1.o.c: Number counting only arrangements whose shape differ from BANANA
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s1.r.c: The number of different shapes we want na 60. 6! also count separate arrangements wey look the same.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s1.o.d: Number of ways to choose 3 of the 6 letters
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s1.r.d: This no be choosing; na arrangement of all 6 in a row.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s1.explain: If we treat dem as six different letters A₁, A₂, A₃, N₁, N₂, B, lining dem up gives 6!=720 ways. But real life, the A letters no different from each other, and same for N, so same shape get counted several times.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite Hyunsu solution in 3 to 4 sentences so younger brother fit understand. Explain why expression turn out that way and give 1 example.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s2.hint.0: To help somebody wey no know expression understand, first state assumption: "if we treat all letters as different."
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s2.hint.1: Write one BANANA arrangement with numbers on the 3 A letters, then write arrangements that become same word when numbers swap.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s2.placeholder: To my brother: the letters of BANANA ...
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: When you use words your brother no know (permutation, factorial), you explain dem?
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: You give example showing say swapping identical letters gives same word?
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You explain why divisors are 3! and 2!?
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s2.model.0: There are 3 A letters, so first we pretend they different and count 6! ways. But swapping the A letters gives same word. There are 3!=6 ways to swap their places, so each word count 6 times. That is why divide by 3!, and divide N letters by 2! for same reason.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s2.model.1: If we color the 3 A letters in BANANA red, blue, yellow, dem become different and we count 6! ways. When we remove colors, arrangements with A swapped become same word. There are 3!=6 ways to swap A places, so groups of 6 arrangements make same word; that is why divide by 3!. N letters come in groups of 2, so divide by 2!.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s2.model.2: If we number letters and treat all different, there are 6!=720 ways, but after removing numbers each word count 12 times. Divide 720 by 12 to get 60 ways. The 12 come from 3! for swapping A letters and 2! for swapping N letters.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s3.prompt: Using same method, how many ways to arrange the 5 letters AABBC in a row?
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s3.hint.0: First write which letters count repeatedly and how many times each repeat.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s3.hint.1: Apply what we did for BANANA to identical letters in this word.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s3.r.a: That na count when A and B all treated as different letters. It no account for swapping identical letters giving same word.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s3.r.b: You divide only A letters by 2! and leave B letters. Since B also get 2 identical letters, divide dem for same reason.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s3.r.c: That na value of 5×4. It no count ways to arrange letters.
n-m-h1-comb-06.s.s3.explain: If all 5 letters be different, there are 5!=120 ways. Each word count 2! ways for swapping A and 2! for swapping B, so 5!÷(2!×2!)=120÷4=30 ways.

n-m-h1-comb-08.title: The chances say two numbers go add up to odd and say dem go add up to even, dem really equal?
n-m-h1-comb-08.topic: Counting: count by odd and even, and the reason for generalizing
n-m-h1-comb-08.goal: Count pairs wey their sum na odd or even by separating odd and even, and understand the difference between small examples wey no fit prove general claim and method wey use letter show am for every case.
n-m-h1-comb-08.material: Minho talk say, “When we choose two different numbers from natural numbers 1 to n, odd and even numbers dey about half-half, so number O of pairs wey their sum na odd and number E of pairs wey their sum na even suppose equal (O=E).” (Order no matter; count the pairs of two numbers wey we choose.)

n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose three different values for n from 4 reach 12, and for each one, count am directly and enter number of odd numbers o, number of even numbers e, number of pairs wey their sum na even E, and number of pairs wey their sum na odd O.

n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s1.hint.1: First decide the parity wey the two numbers must get for their sum to be even, then count am using number of odd and even numbers.

n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s1.fail.c1: n must be integer from 4 reach 12.

n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s1.explain: n=4: E=2, O=4. n=5: E=4, O=6. n=6: E=6, O=9. For the sum to be odd, you must choose one odd and one even number, so O=o×e; for the sum to be even, you must choose two odd numbers or two even numbers, so E=C(o, 2)+C(e, 2).
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s2.prompt: All three times, pairs wey their sum na odd plenty pass (O>E). How we suppose judge Minho claim and this result?
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s2.hint.0: Think whether one example fit show say Minho claim no correct, or na all cases e need.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the new claim “for every n there are more odd sums” don get proof from three examples.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s2.o.a: Every one of the three times O≠E, so Minho wrong, and we fit also talk say for any n odd sums must plenty pass.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s2.r.a: Counterexample don show say Minho claim no correct. But only three results no fit prove say odd sums plenty pass for every n.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s2.o.b: Odd and even numbers almost equal for number, so we fit treat this small difference like error and talk say Minho claim (O=E) correct.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s2.r.b: Minho claim say O and E “equal”. If O and E wey you count directly no equal, the claim no correct for that n. You no fit save the claim by calling the difference “error”.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s2.o.c: For the three values wey I choose, O≠E, so dem be counterexamples to Minho claim (O=E), but to talk say odd sums plenty pass for every n, we gats show am separately with letter.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s2.o.d: As n dey grow, difference O−E between O and E dey reduce and at last e go become O=E.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s2.r.d: For n=4, 6, 8, O−E na 2, 3, 4, and e dey grow in fact. You no fit use small number of examples talk wetin go happen when n don big.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s2.explain: Since the claim na general (all n), one counterexample fit show say e false. But the new claim “for every n there are more odd sums” no get proof from small number of examples, so we gats use letter show am.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s3.prompt: When n=2k (k na natural number), k odd numbers and k even numbers dey. Write number O of pairs wey their sum na odd and number E of pairs wey their sum na even using k, find O−E, and show say odd sums plenty pass.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s3.hint.0: First write the parity wey the two numbers we choose must get for their sum to be odd.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s3.hint.1: Write O and E using k, simplify their difference, then check the sign.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You explain why choosing one odd and one even number gives O?
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You separate E into two cases, choosing two numbers with the same parity, and add dem?
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You talk say since k na natural number, O−E always positive?
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s3.model.0: For the sum to be odd, we gats choose one odd and one even number, so O=k×k=k². For the sum to be even, we choose two odds or two evens, so E=C(k,2)+C(k,2)=k(k−1). O−E=k²−k(k−1)=k, and since k na natural number e always positive, so odd sums plenty pass.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s3.model.1: O na k×k=k² ways, by choosing one of k odd numbers and one of k even numbers. E na k(k−1) ways, the sum of k(k−1)/2 ways to choose two odds and k(k−1)/2 ways to choose two evens. Difference O−E=k>0, so odd sums plenty pass by k.
n-m-h1-comb-08.s.s3.model.2: O na k×k=k² ways, by choosing one of k odd numbers and one of k even numbers, and E na k(k−1) ways. So O always bigger than E by k.

n-m-h1-func-08.s.s3.prompt: Find the correct solution of inequality (x+3)/(x−1) ≥ 2, and explain one method to find am.

n-m-h1-mat-01.title: Find 2×2 matrices wey satisfy A²=−E
n-m-h1-mat-01.goal: Turn equation A²=−E into conditions on entries, make matrices wey satisfy am yourself, then explain wetin your examples share and why.
n-m-h1-mat-01.material: For real number x, no real x dey wey x²=−1. So how about 2×2 matrices A wey A²=−E? Here matrix [[a,b],[c,d]] na 2×2 matrix wey first row na a, b and second row na c, d. E na identity matrix [[1,0],[0,1]]. −E na [[−1,0],[0,−1]]. Use integer entries only.
n-m-h1-mat-01.thinking.0: Check whether idea from real numbers (square no fit negative) fit apply to matrices same way
n-m-h1-mat-01.thinking.1: Turn matrix equation into equations for entries and make examples
n-m-h1-mat-01.thinking.2: Find structure wey examples share and explain why by splitting cases
n-m-h1-mat-01.prereq.0: How to find (i,j) entry in matrix multiplication
n-m-h1-mat-01.prereq.1: Say −E na identity matrix with sign of every entry changed
n-m-h1-mat-01.prereq.2: Split into cases for when product equal 0
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose correct entries of square A²=A×A for A=[[a,b],[c,d]]. (Entry (1,1) na cell for first row and first column, and (1,2) na cell for first row and second column.)
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s1.hint.0: Instead of a, b, c, d, put numbers like 1, 2, 3, 4 and calculate A×A directly, then compare with value wey you get if you put same numbers inside formula for each option.
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s1.hint.1: Mark which row and column of A you pair, multiply, and add to get (1,2) entry.
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s1.r.a: E square each cell separately. Matrix multiplication pair one row with one column, multiply dem, then add, wey different from squaring each cell.
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s1.r.c: The (1,1) entry correct, but for (1,2) e pair first row and second column wrong. First row na (a, b), and second column na (b, d).
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s1.r.d: E pair the first row with itself. For (1,1), the first row (a, b) must pair with first column (a, c).
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s1.explain: If we pair first row (a, b) with first column (a, c), we get (1,1) entry a·a+b·c=a²+bc; pairing am with second column (b, d) gives (1,2) entry a·b+b·d=b(a+d). Same way, (2,1) entry na c(a+d) and (2,2) entry na d²+bc.
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter three different sets of integers a, b, c, d wey make A²=−E, that is, four cells of A² be −1, 0, 0, −1 in order.
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write equations for condition say the (1,2) entry and (2,1) entry must be 0, then separate cases where one product equal 0.
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether b and c fit both be 0, and if no, find a and d for the other cases.
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s2.explain: For example, if A=[[0,−1],[1,0]], then A²=[[−1,0],[0,−1]]=−E. No real number x fit satisfy x²=−1, but some matrices fit, and many such matrices dey. [[0,1],[1,0]] no work because its square na E, and E or −E no work too because their squares na E.
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Compare examples wey you make, find and write relationship between a and d wey hold for all, and explain why that relationship must be needed.
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: For every example, calculate values like a+d, a−d, and a×d, write dem side by side, then compare wetin remain the same.
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write conditions for (1,2) and (2,1) entries of A² to be 0, and think whether b and c fit both be 0.
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: You calculate a+d yourself for each example wey you make?
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: You consider separately the case where b and c both be 0?
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: From condition on (1,2) entry, you fit explain which number multiply another to get 0?
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s2.because.model.0: For every example, a+d=0, that is, d=−a. The (1,2) entry na b(a+d)=0 and (2,1) entry na c(a+d)=0, but if b=c=0, then a²=−1, wey impossible, so at least one of b and c no be 0, and then a+d must be 0.
n-m-h1-mat-01.s.s2.because.model.1: a and d get opposite signs (their sum na 0). If b and c both be 0, then a squared go need equal −1, and no real number fit do that, so b or c no be 0, and then b(a+d)=0 or c(a+d)=0 give a+d=0.

n-m-h1-mat-02.title: (AB)C and A(BC): same result, but the work amount same?
n-m-h1-mat-02.topic: Matrices: associativity and amount of calculation
n-m-h1-mat-02.goal: Even though associativity gives same result, use multiplication count check say amount of calculation fit differ depending how product group, and design sizes wey make the calculation amount differ plenty.
n-m-h1-mat-02.material: Matrix multiplication associative, (AB)C=A(BC), so result matrix same no matter which product you calculate first. But amount of work to do, e too same? If we multiply p×q matrix (p rows, q columns) with q×r matrix, result na p×r matrix, and every cell need q multiplications, so altogether p×q×r multiplications dey. Let A be p×q matrix, B a q×r matrix, and C an r×s matrix, and count only multiplications (no need count additions).
n-m-h1-mat-02.thinking.0: Tell apart fact say results same from fact say process costs same
n-m-h1-mat-02.thinking.1: Set sizes as variables and write expressions to design cases wey satisfy condition
n-m-h1-mat-02.thinking.2: Choose calculation order based on sizes of intermediate results
n-m-h1-mat-02.prereq.0: Size condition for matrix product to be defined
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s1.prompt: When A na 2×3, B na 3×4, and C na 4×1, choose correct comparison of multiplication counts for two methods. ((AB)C calculate AB first, then multiply by C; A(BC) calculate BC first, then multiply A by am.)
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s1.hint.0: For (AB)C, write size of AB wey you make first, and add multiplication count for product of that AB with C.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s1.hint.1: For A(BC) too, write size of BC and add the two multiplication counts the same way.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s1.o.a: (AB)C need 24 and A(BC) need 12, so A(BC) need fewer
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s1.r.a: E count only the first multiplication for each method. You must count the second multiplication too (multiplying remaining matrix into the result).
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s1.o.b: (AB)C need 18 and A(BC) need 32, so (AB)C need fewer
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s1.r.b: The numbers for the two methods don swap. Check again the size of intermediate matrix each method create.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s1.o.c: (AB)C need 32 and A(BC) need 18, so A(BC) need fewer
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s1.o.d: The results na the same, so (AB)C and A(BC) need same multiplication count
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s1.r.d: E treat “result matrix na the same” and “calculation amount na the same” like the same claim. If intermediate matrices get different sizes, multiplication counts too go differ.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s1.explain: (AB)C: AB na 2×4 and need 2·3·4=24 multiplications, then (2×4)(4×1) need 2·4·1=8, total na 32. A(BC): BC na 3×1 and need 3·4·1=12, then (2×3)(3×1) need 2·3·1=6, total na 18.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter two different sets of sizes p, q, r, s (each na integer from 1 to 10) wey make (AB)C need at least twice the multiplications of A(BC).
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write as expressions the multiplication number for (AB)C, p·q·r+p·r·s, and for A(BC), q·r·s+p·q·s.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s2.hint.1: Put some numbers to compare which expression reduce more when s very small.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s2.var.q: q (number of columns for A = number of rows for B)
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s2.var.r: r (number of columns for B = number of rows for C)
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s2.ok.c1: All four numbers na integers from 1 reach 10.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s2.fail.c1: All four numbers must be integers from 1 reach 10.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s2.ok.c2: Multiplication number for (AB)C at least twice the one for A(BC).
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Multiplication number for (AB)C smaller than twice the one for A(BC).
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s2.explain: For example, if p=3, q=3, r=9, s=1, then (AB)C need 81+27=108 and A(BC) need 27+9=36, so na 3 times. The (2,3,4,1) from earlier step gives 32 and 18, less than 2 times; for (1,5,5,5), na A(BC) need more.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s3.prompt: Explain why multiplication numbers different even though (AB)C and A(BC) give same result. Then choose one of the sizes you enter and write which product better to calculate first for those sizes, giving sizes of intermediate matrices and your reason.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write the size of intermediate matrix wey each method make first, and compare dem.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s3.hint.1: Find how number of cells in intermediate matrix connect to multiplication count.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You distinguish both say results same and calculation amounts different?
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You give intermediate matrix sizes as evidence?
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You explain your chosen order for the sizes you enter, with intermediate matrix sizes?
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s3.model.0: By associativity, result matrix same whichever product you calculate first. But first intermediate matrix get different size, so multiplication counts different. If p=3, q=3, r=9, s=1, then AB na big 3×9, but BC na small 3×1, so A(BC), wey calculate BC first, need 36, much fewer than 108 for (AB)C.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s3.model.1: Result same, but calculation amount different. Bigger intermediate matrix need more multiplications for next product, so choose method wey make intermediate matrix small, multiplying B and C first (A(BC)).
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s3.model.2: (AB) become big matrix, but BC small matrix with one column only. So A(BC) better because e need fewer multiplications.
n-m-h1-mat-02.s.s3.model.3: Result same, but multiplication counts different. If C get one column, multiplying BC first to make small intermediate matrix need fewer multiplications.

n-m-h1-mat-03.title: Find k wey make inverse matrix exist: check Kyuri solution
n-m-h1-mat-03.topic: Matrices: condition for inverse matrix to exist, and letter k
n-m-h1-mat-03.goal: Compare condition (inverse matrix exist) with direction of expressions wey solution use, find and correct error, then check by putting values to write correct range.
n-m-h1-mat-03.material: Kyuri want find real k values wey make matrix A=[[k,3],[2,k+1]] get inverse. (A 2×2 matrix [[a,b],[c,d]] get inverse only when ad−bc no be 0. Matrix [[k,3],[2,k+1]] get first row k, 3 and second row 2, k+1.) Kyuri solution na this.

n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s1.hint.1: Put symbol for condition we set up in first line beside symbol for equation we solve afterward, then compare dem.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s1.line.0: For inverse matrix to exist, ad−bc≠0 must hold.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s1.line.2: So k²+k−6=0 must hold, and from (k−2)(k+3)=0, k=2 or k=−3.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s1.line.3: So k values we want na 2 and −3.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s1.explain: Line 3 na first wrong line. Line 1 say ad−bc≠0 must hold, but line 3 find k values wey make ad−bc=0. Calculation k²+k−6 for line 2 correct, and line 4 just copy result of line 3.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s2.prompt: Correct Kyuri solution and choose the most accurate description of k range wey make inverse matrix exist.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s2.hint.0: First find k values wey make k²+k−6=(k−2)(k+3) equal 0, then judge whether inverse exist for those values.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s2.hint.1: Put k=0, k=2, k=−3, and k=5 inside, make table of cases wey get inverse, then compare with choices.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s2.r.a: Dem solve using “or.” This condition too hold when k=2 (because k≠−3 true), so e include k=2. The connective wey mean both must fail na “and.”
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s2.r.b: These na values where ad−bc=0. At these values inverse no dey. It swap the cases wey get inverse with the ones wey no get.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s2.r.d: E lose sign when finding roots of k²+k−6=0. The k wey make (k+3)=0 na −3.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s2.explain: Inverse no dey only when k=2 and k=−3, where ad−bc=(k−2)(k+3) equal 0. So when k na any real number apart from 2 and −3, inverse dey.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s3.prompt: Put k=2 and k=1 inside A and calculate ad−bc to show why Kyuri answer wrong. Then write correct k range in one sentence.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write matrix for each of k=2 and k=1, then calculate ad−bc.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s3.hint.1: Say in words which of the two results relate to “inverse exists.”
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You substitute both values and calculate ad−bc yourself?
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You say how the value wey give 0 and the one wey no give 0 each connect to whether inverse exist?
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s3.model.0: If k=2, then ad−bc=2×3−3×2=0, so inverse no dey. If k=1, then ad−bc=1×2−3×2=−4, wey no be 0, so inverse dey. So 2 and −3 wey Kyuri find na values wey inverse no dey, and correct answer na k≠2 and k≠−3.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s3.model.1: Putting k=2 make ad−bc equal 0, so inverse no dey. But if k=1, e be −4, so inverse dey. Therefore remove 2 and −3, and answer na all real numbers apart from 2 and −3.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s3.model.2: If k=2, ad−bc na 0, so inverse no dey; if k=1, e be −4, so inverse dey. So remove 2 and −3.
n-m-h1-mat-03.s.s3.model.3: Putting k=2 gives ad−bc=0, and putting k=1 gives −4. So k must be neither 2 nor −3.

n-m-h1-mat-04.title: How Market Share Change Each Month? When Information Show One Part at a Time
n-m-h1-mat-04.topic: Matrices: changes in market share and repeated matrix multiplication
n-m-h1-mat-04.goal: Use matrix to write movement rule, calculate month by month to correct intuitive prediction (increase by same amount every time), and find share wey no change using equation.
n-m-h1-mat-04.material: Two phone companies dey, 가 and 나. In one month, 90% of subscribers for 가 stay, and 10% move to 나. 80% of subscribers for 나 stay, and 20% move to 가. This movement rule same every month. Written as matrix P=[[0.9, 0.1],[0.2, 0.8]], first row show proportions moving from 가 to (가, 나), and second row from 나 to (가, 나). Starting shares na 60% for 가 and 40% for 나. Assume total subscriber number no change.

n-m-h1-mat-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Both months, 6.0% and 8.0% moved; difference between 63.4% and 64% na rounding error.
n-m-h1-mat-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Shares change in second month, so number moving changes too. Rounding no explain the difference.

n-m-h1-logic-05.title: Wetin more we need know if all we know na “If e rain, dem cancel am”?
n-m-h1-logic-05.goal: When “if p, then q” true, work out what information we need to surely conclude “if q, then p,” and use contrapositive explain why that information enough.
n-m-h1-logic-05.material: One school rule talk say “If e rain, dem cancel outdoor class,” and dem follow this rule every time. Mina want say as always true, “If dem cancel outdoor class, then the day rain.” For this rule, p na “Rain dey” and q na “Dem cancel outdoor class.”
n-m-h1-logic-05.thinking.0: Separate wetin we already know from new facts
n-m-h1-logic-05.thinking.1: Understand how converse and inverse relate
n-m-h1-logic-05.prereq.0: Converse, inverse, and contrapositive of proposition p→q
n-m-h1-logic-05.prereq.1: Contrapositive get the same truth value as original proposition
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the fact apart from the rule we need, to be sure Mina conclusion always true.
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s1.hint.0: First write the conclusion Mina want state in the form “If □, then □,” using p and q.
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s1.hint.1: Rewrite each choice in the same form, then decide whether e already follow from the rule or na new information.
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s1.o.a: For days wey dem hold outdoor class, rain no fall
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s1.r.a: Dis statement na contrapositive of ‘If rain fall, dem cancel class.’ Di rule already imply am, so e no be new information.
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s1.o.b: For di past month, every day wey dem cancel class na rainy day
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s1.r.b: Wetin happen for recent times no guarantee say e go always happen like dat for future. We need rule wey always hold.
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s1.o.c: If rain no fall, dem no cancel outdoor class
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s1.o.d: Rainy days no pass ten for one month
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s1.r.d: How many rainy days dey no get connection with ‘If dem cancel am, then rain fall.’
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s1.explain: Mina conclusion na q→p (di converse). ‘If rain no fall, dem no cancel class’ na ~p→~q (di inverse), and its contrapositive na exactly q→p. So if di inverse always true, di converse go always true too. Option a na just contrapositive of original rule and no add information, and b and d no be rules wey always hold or no connect.
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s2.prompt: Use di fact wey you choose explain in two or three sentences why Mina conclusion always hold. Use di word ‘contrapositive.’
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s2.hint.0: Write di fact wey you choose as ‘If □, then □,’ then swap di condition and conclusion and negate both.
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s2.hint.1: Compare di sentence wey you make with Mina conclusion to check whether dem be di same.
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s2.placeholder: e.g., Di contrapositive of ‘If rain no fall, dem no cancel class’ na ...
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: When you make di contrapositive, you change both ‘~’ signs?
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: When you make di contrapositive, you flip di ‘~’ for both parts?
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: You also talk say di original rule by itself no guarantee dis conclusion?
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s2.model.0: Di contrapositive of ‘If rain no fall, dem no cancel class’ na ‘If dem cancel class, then rain fall.’ Contrapositive always get di same truth value as original statement, so Mina conclusion always hold.
n-m-h1-logic-05.s.s2.model.1: Dat fact mean if ~p, then ~q, and its contrapositive na: if q, then p, dat is, if dem cancel class, na rainy day. Contrapositive get di same truth value as original proposition, so conclusion sure.

n-m-h1-logic-07.title: Find two numbers wey their multiple sets join together get 12 elements
n-m-h1-logic-07.goal: Count elements for union of multiple sets of two numbers with inclusion-exclusion, and use fact say common elements na multiples of least common multiple to find two numbers wey satisfy di condition.
n-m-h1-logic-07.material: Among natural numbers from 1 to 60, make A be set of multiples of a and B be set of multiples of b. For example, if a=4, then A={4, 8, 12, …, 60}.
n-m-h1-logic-07.thinking.0: Rewrite number of elements for union using number of elements for intersection
n-m-h1-logic-07.thinking.2: Find some solutions and check dem
n-m-h1-logic-07.prereq.1: Multiples, common multiples, and least common multiple
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s1.prompt: When a=6 and b=15, choose statement wey describe elements of A∩B exactly.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s1.hint.0: List some numbers yourself, starting from smallest, wey be multiples of both 6 and 15.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s1.hint.1: Look at numbers you find and see whose multiples dem form.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s1.o.a: Dem na multiples of 90, so no one from 1 to 60
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s1.r.a: E use product 6×15 as basis for common multiples. E no check whether smaller common multiple dey.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s1.o.b: E equal di smaller number of multiples of 6 and multiples of 15
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s1.r.b: E treat smaller size of both multiple sets as intersection size. E no find overlapping numbers directly.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s1.o.c: Dem na multiples of 30, so two dey: 30 and 60
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s1.o.d: Dem na multiples of 3, so 20 dey
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s1.r.d: E use 3, di common divisor of 6 and 15, as basis. If number na multiple of 3, dat no mean say e be multiple of both 6 and 15.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s1.explain: Numbers wey be multiples of both 6 and 15 na multiples of their least common multiple, 30. From 1 to 60, two dey: 30 and 60. If you count dem as multiples of 6×15=90, you wrongly get none.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.prompt: Enter two different pairs of natural numbers a, b where n(A∪B)=12. Conditions: 2≤a<b≤20, a and b no be coprime, and b no be multiple of a.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.hint.0: For each a, first find n(A)=⌊60÷a⌋, then check whether adding both set sizes and subtracting overlap give 12.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.hint.1: Find overlap using least common multiple. Choose some possible (a, b) and make calculation table to compare.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b na natural numbers and 2≤a<b≤20.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Dem must be natural numbers, with 2≤a<b≤20.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.ok.c2: Dem no be coprime, and b no be multiple of a.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.fail.c2: Dem must no be coprime, and b must no be multiple of a.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.explain: (6, 15): 10+4−2=12, (6, 16): 10+3−1=12, (6, 20): 10+3−1=12, (8, 10): 7+6−1=12. For dis range, na only these four pairs dey. If you count overlap as multiples of a×b, then (6, 15) give 10+4−0=14, wey wrong.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.because.prompt: For (a, b)=(6, 15), explain why you must no count common elements as multiples of 6×15=90.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write multiples of 6 and multiples of 15 up to 60, then find numbers dem share.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare whether those numbers less or greater than 90.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g., Common multiples of 6 and 15 na ..., so ...
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: You find least common multiple of 6 and 15 yourself?
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: You talk say 90 na just one common multiple, e no be smallest?
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.because.model.0: Least common multiple of 6 and 15 na 30. So 30 and 60 too be multiples of both; if you count only multiples of 90, you miss both and get wrong answer.
n-m-h1-logic-07.s.s2.because.model.1: Number wey be multiple of both 6 and 15 na multiple of least common multiple, 30. 90 na just one of dem, so if na only am we use, we no count 30 and 60 as common elements.

n-m-h1-logic-08.title: How we go decide whether ‘for every x’ proposition true or false?
n-m-h1-logic-08.goal: Decide whether proposition wey start ‘for every x’ true or false using one counterexample or full argument, no be some examples; write its negation correctly and think about boundary values.
n-m-h1-logic-08.material:
Proposition P: ‘For all real numbers x, x²−4x+k>0.’ (k na constant.) Three friends decide whether P true or false when k=4 like dis.
- Jiho: I put x=0, 1, 3, 5 inside and every value greater than 0, so true.
- Seoyeon: x²−4x+4=(x−2)², and square at least 0, so always greater than 0. True.
- Daeun: If I put x=2, value na 0, wey no greater than 0. False.
n-m-h1-logic-08.thinking.0: Separate some values you check from all values
n-m-h1-logic-08.thinking.2: Decide whether boundary values dey included
n-m-h1-logic-08.prereq.1: Perfect-square expressions and minimum of quadratic
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s1.prompt: When k=4, choose correct truth value of P together with correct reason.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s1.hint.0: Separate whether each friend reasoning ‘check some values’ or ‘cover every value.’
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s1.hint.1: Find smallest value of expression Seoyeon write, then compare am with ‘greater than 0.’
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s1.o.a: True: because e hold for all di few values I try
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s1.r.a: E replace ‘all real numbers’ with some values wey dem check. Some values still never check.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s1.o.b: True: square always at least 0, so expression value greater than 0
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s1.r.b: E change ‘at least 0’ to ‘greater than 0.’ E miss di case where equal sign hold.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s1.o.c: False: one real number make expression equal 0, wey break ‘greater than 0 for all real numbers’
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s1.o.d: Cannot tell: real numbers dey infinite, so e impossible to check dem all
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s1.r.d: E assume say na only by checking one value at a time we fit decide. You fit decide with one counterexample or expression structure.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s1.explain: Proposition ‘for all real numbers x’ false if even one x (counterexample) no work. When k=4, expression na (x−2)², and at x=2 e become 0, so ‘greater than 0’ no hold; therefore P false. Jiho method check only some values, and Seoyeon confuse ‘at least 0’ with ‘greater than 0.’
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s2.prompt: Choose di negation of proposition P.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s2.hint.0: Think how many x values must fail for ‘for all …, …’ to be false.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s2.hint.1: Check wetin be negation of ‘>’ inequality and which side equality to 0 dey.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s2.o.a: For all real numbers x, x²−4x+k<0
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s2.r.a: E keep ‘for all’ as e be and write negation of ‘>’ as only ‘<’. Both parts wrong.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s2.o.b: For all real numbers x, x²−4x+k≤0
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s2.r.b: E keep ‘for all’ as negation of ‘for all’ and only change inequality sign. E miss say one failed case don make statement false.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s2.o.c: One real number x dey such that x²−4x+k<0
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s2.r.c: E write negation of ‘>’ as only ‘<’. E miss case where value na 0.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s2.o.d: One real number x dey such that x²−4x+k≤0
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s2.explain: Negation of ‘for all x, A’ na ‘one x dey such that not A.’ Negation of ‘>0’ na ‘≤0’ (no pass 0), so negation na: one real x dey such that x²−4x+k≤0. When k=4, dis negation true at x=2, wey agree with judgment say P false.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s3.prompt: Write k values wey make P true, and explain in one sentence why k=4 no dey inside di range.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s3.hint.0: Rewrite x²−4x+k so you fit see (x−2)², then express minimum value using k.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s3.hint.1: Compare with condition ‘>0’ to decide whether minimum must be greater than 0 or only at least 0.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., k range na ..., and if k=4, then x=...
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You rewrite expression as (x−2)²+k−4 and find minimum?
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You choose range based on fact say minimum must be greater than 0?
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You show with one x value why ‘>’ fail at boundary?
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s3.model.0: x²−4x+k=(x−2)²+k−4 and minimum na k−4, so e always greater than 0 when k>4. If k=4, value na 0 at x=2, so e no greater than 0 and k=4 no dey included.
n-m-h1-logic-08.s.s3.model.1: Discriminant 16−4k must be negative, so k must greater than 4. If k=4, discriminant na 0, so expression value na 0 when x=2, and P false.
